curation_notes: This draft aggressively merges repetitive week-5 pandas snippets into exam-usable parent-topic summaries.
Weak one-line duplicates and low-signal micro-snippets were omitted unless they added a concrete exam distinction.

main_topics.title: Pandas Core Structures

must_know.title: Know the three base objects cold: `Series`, `DataFrame`, and the default index
must_know.summary: A `Series` is one labeled column of data. A `DataFrame` is a 2D table built most often from a dict of equal-length lists. If you do not supply an index, pandas gives `0, 1, 2, ...` automatically.
must_know.example:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([153, 160, 150], name='Length')
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
must_know.why_kept: This is foundational and cleaner than shipping several separate low-value constructor snippets.

content.text: A DataFrame is most often built from a dict of equal-length lists.

must_know.title: Shape rule that keeps appearing on exams: `df['A']` vs `df[['A']]`
must_know.summary: `df['A']` returns a `Series` (1D). `df[['A']]` returns a one-column `DataFrame` (2D). Use the list form whenever the question explicitly wants a DataFrame back.
must_know.example:
df['A']        # Series
df[['A']]      # one-column DataFrame
df[['A', 'B']] # two-column DataFrame
must_know.why_kept: This is one of the highest-payoff pandas distinctions and should be stated once, clearly, instead of repeated in fragmented forms.

content.text: When the prompt explicitly wants a DataFrame back, keep the selection 2D.

must_know.title: Use direct column arithmetic for derived columns before reaching for `map` or `apply`
must_know.summary: If the task is plain elementwise column math, write the vectorized expression directly. Do not wrap simple column addition or subtraction in `map(...)` or row-wise `apply(...)` unless the question truly needs custom per-value or per-row logic.
must_know.why_kept: This merges the strongest Week 5 pattern with the most common mistake pattern.
source_basis: exam-Trial final exam Introduction to Python-5-w5-pandas-core-structures

exam_patterns.title: Creating a new column from existing columns
exam_patterns.summary: Exam questions repeatedly test whether you understand that new columns are assigned by column name and filled with vectorized Series results.
exam_patterns.pattern:
df['C'] = df['A'] + df['B']
# or
df.loc[:, 'C'] = df.loc[:, 'A'] + df.loc[:, 'B']
watch_out: Do not use a row label like `df.loc['C']` when the goal is a new column.
source_basis: exam-Trial final exam Introduction to Python-5-w5-pandas-core-structures

exam_patterns.title: The classic trap: `map` is not a shortcut for vectorized arithmetic
exam_patterns.summary: `Series.map(...)` expects a function, dict, or mapping-like Series. If the whole expression already works elementwise, use the vectorized form directly.

useful_backup.title: Index alignment can silently create `NaN` values
useful_backup.summary: When pandas combines Series or DataFrames, it aligns by index labels. If indices do not match, the result can fill with `NaN` instead of doing row-by-row arithmetic by position.
useful_backup.why_backup: Useful and exam-relevant, but less core than constructors, shape, and direct column arithmetic.

useful_backup.title: DatetimeIndex matters only when the index actually stores dates
useful_backup.summary: If the DataFrame index is a `DatetimeIndex`, rows can be filtered using date attributes like `.month`. This is worth keeping as a backup, not a headline rule.
useful_backup.example: df.loc[[r for r in df.index if r.month == 4]]
useful_backup.why_backup: Legitimate pattern, but too specialized to sit in shipped must-know content.

dropped_or_merged: Merged repeated constructor/alias snippets into one clean basics rule.
Dropped noisy dataframe-mutation examples that are harder to memorize than they are worth for the UI.

main_topics.title: Inspecting and Selecting Data

must_know.title: Selection rule in one sentence: plain `df[...]` is not for two axes
must_know.summary: Use plain `df[...]` for column selection or a boolean row mask. The moment both a row selector and a column selector appear, switch to `.loc[row_sel, col_sel]` or `.iloc[row_sel, col_sel]`.
must_know.why_kept: This is the clearest repeated weakness and should be shipped as a flagship snippet.

must_know.title: Know the `loc` vs `iloc` slicing difference exactly
must_know.summary: `.loc` is label-based and includes the stop label in a slice. `.iloc` is integer-position based and excludes the stop position, like normal Python slicing.
must_know.why_kept: Students confuse these constantly, and the distinction directly affects exam answers.

must_know.title: Selection shape is part of the answer, not a side detail
must_know.summary: A scalar selector often collapses the result to a `Series`; wrapping labels in a list usually keeps a `DataFrame`. When the prompt says 'return a DataFrame', preserve 2D shape intentionally.
must_know.example:
df.loc[2]      # Series
df.loc[[2]]    # DataFrame
df.loc[df.index % 2 == 0, ['B']]  # DataFrame, not Series
must_know.why_kept: Several exam questions turn entirely on result shape.
source_basis: exam-Trial final exam Introduction to Python-6-w5-inspecting-and-selecting-data

must_know.title: Valid vs invalid two-axis selection
must_know.summary: This is the table that helps you reject impossible pandas indexing forms immediately.

rows: plain df[...] is not for two axes
content.text: Switch to `.loc[...]` or `.iloc[...]` as soon as you need both rows and columns.

exam_patterns.title: Select one column for rows that satisfy a row rule
exam_patterns.summary: Build the row condition first, then choose the target column(s). If the task wants a DataFrame, keep the column selector as a list.
watch_out: `df.loc[2::2, 'B']` may return a Series instead of the required DataFrame.
source_basis: exam-Trial final exam Introduction to Python-6-w5-inspecting-and-selecting-data

exam_patterns.title: Boolean mask plus explicit columns is the safest exam default
exam_patterns.summary: When the prompt mixes filtering and selection, `df.loc[mask, columns]` is usually the clearest and least error-prone form.

useful_backup.title: Quick inspection helpers
useful_backup.summary: Use `.head(n)` and `.tail(n)` to inspect rows and `.describe()` for summary statistics. These are useful, but they should stay backup material rather than taking premium UI space.
useful_backup.why_backup: Helpful for orientation, but rarely the decisive concept in multiple-choice exam questions.

Dropped low-value toy indexing examples that repeat the same distinction without adding a new exam pattern.

main_topics.title: Working With Values

must_know.title: Default mental model: vectorized column expressions first, `map`/`apply` only when needed
must_know.summary: If the job is straightforward arithmetic or string work that pandas already supports elementwise, write the expression directly. Use `Series.map(...)` for one value in -> one value out on a single Series. Use `DataFrame.apply(..., axis=1)` only when the logic genuinely needs multiple columns from the same row.
must_know.example:
df['total'] = df['A'] + df['B']
s.map(lambda x: x + 1)
df.apply(lambda row: row['A'] + row['B'], axis=1)
must_know.why_kept: This merges the strongest surviving Week 5 value-transformation rules into one exam-usable decision rule.

must_know.title: Filter first, then aggregate or sort
must_know.summary: A very common exam pattern is: build a mask, select rows or one column, then run `sum()`, `mean()`, `count()`, or `sort_values(...)` on the result.
must_know.example:
mask = df['A'] > 0
result = df.loc[mask, 'B'].mean()
df.sort_values('B', ascending=False)
must_know.why_kept: This is one of the most reusable pandas exam workflows and deserves its own must-know summary.

must_know.title: Use the vectorized text tools pandas already gives you
must_know.summary: Use `.str` methods for built-in string operations over a whole Series, and `isin(...)` for membership tests over many values at once.
must_know.why_kept: This is clearer and more compact than shipping separate tiny snippets for `.str`, `isin`, and string filtering.

must_know.title: Choose between vectorized math, `map`, and `apply` with a quick table
must_know.summary: This restores one of the high-value decision aids that is easy to scan under exam pressure.

rows: one value in -> one value out on a Series
content.text: Use the simplest shape-preserving option that matches the task.

exam_patterns.title: Text splitting: choose output shape on purpose
exam_patterns.summary: If you want one derived Series, `map(...)` can be enough. If you want multiple new DataFrame columns, use `.str.split(..., expand=True)`.
exam_patterns.pattern:
s.map(lambda x: x.split('; ')[0])
# or
df[['municipality', 'province']] = df['place'].str.split('; ', expand=True)
watch_out: Do not treat `Series.split(...)` as if pandas strings worked like plain Python strings.
Choose `expand=True` only when the target is multiple columns.

exam_patterns.title: Missing values: decide whether to keep shape or drop data
exam_patterns.summary: Use `.fillna(...)` if you want to preserve the table and replace missing values. Use `.dropna()` when incomplete rows or columns should disappear entirely.

useful_backup.title: Sorting and scalar broadcasting are good support patterns, not front-page content
useful_backup.summary: Keep `sort_values(...)` vs `sort_index(...)` and scalar broadcasting in reserve because they matter, but they are less often the decisive snippet than filtering, shape, and map/apply decisions.
useful_backup.why_backup: These belong in backup because they are useful follow-ups, not the clearest parent-topic anchors.

dropped_or_merged: Merged separate snippets for sort, map, apply, isin, and string methods into a smaller set of decision rules.
Dropped weak standalone one-liners such as isolated `drop(...)`/`dropna()` examples unless they supported a broader exam pattern.
